title: Choosing the Gains: What Each One Costs, Measured

questions.question: Raising the proportional gain from 2 to 20 on the same loop. What happens, measured?
options: The rise time falls from 0.86 to 0.24 seconds and the overshoot rises from 51 to 81 percent
Both the rise time and the overshoot improve
The rise time improves and nothing else changes
The loop becomes more accurate at the target
questions.explanation: More proportional gain is a trade rather than an improvement. At twenty it is fast and never stops ringing.

questions.question: What does derivative gain buy and what does it cost?
options: It removes the overshoot and slows the rise, and it is what makes an aggressive loop settle at all
It removes the steady state error at no cost
It makes the rise faster and the overshoot larger
It has no effect until the loop is at the target
questions.explanation: Measured: P 20 alone never settles, and P 20 with a derivative of 8 settles in 1.21 seconds with no overshoot, having given up about half a second of rise time.

questions.question: A loop with no steady load is given an integral term. What happens?
options: It gets worse: overshoot appears where there was none and settling takes five times longer
Nothing, since there is no steady state error for it to act on
The rise time improves
It becomes more robust to disturbance
questions.explanation: The term accumulates on the way to the target, so it still holds a value when the error reaches zero and keeps pushing until an error of the opposite sign cancels it. That is what the overshoot is.

questions.question: A joint with a five newton load and a proportional gain of twenty stops 0.25 short. Why exactly that?
options: Proportional output exists only while there is error, so it stops at the error that produces the force the load needs: the load over the gain
The derivative term is opposing it
The output limits were reached
The measurement is biased by the load
questions.explanation: Five over twenty is 0.25, and no amount of derivative gain changes it, because the derivative term is zero once the thing has stopped moving.

questions.question: Why is settling time the last exit from the band rather than the first entry?
options: An oscillating response passes through the band on its way past the target, so the first entry is near the start with all the ringing still to come
The first entry is harder to compute
The band is only valid after the peak
They give the same answer for any real response
questions.explanation: The worse a loop rings, the earlier the wrong version reports it as settled, and the error is in the flattering direction, which is the direction nobody questions.

questions.question: How do you decide whether a loop needs an integral term at all?
options: Run it with P and D only and look at where it stops: if it stops on the target, there is nothing for an integral term to do
Always add one, then tune it down
Add one if the rise time is too slow
Add one whenever the plant has damping
questions.explanation: The question is about the machine rather than the controller: is there something needing a constant force just to hold still. One experiment answers it.
